sections.value:
A list has been going round: fifteen projects every AI security engineer "must build", and a
twelve-stage curriculum to go with them. A Crescendo fuzzer, a sandboxed MCP proxy, an
inter-agent sanitization bus, a PII-swapping gateway, a grammar-caged output layer, an OAuth
broker for agents, a PyRIT gate in CI, a hash-chained audit ledger, and so on down to
activation patching and published CVEs.

Its instinct is right. This is a field you learn by building, and almost every item names a real
attack surface. But a list cannot tell you which items carry weight, in what order to build them,
or why. Several of its one-line "why"s rest on premises that the 2025–2026 evidence contradicts.
Some of those projects would be built to defend the wrong layer.

This post derives the field from a single fact and then walks the path an attacker's text takes
through an agent: in, through the decision, out to a tool, out of the system. Each of the fifteen
projects gets placed where it belongs on that path, kept, reframed or demoted, with the evidence
for each call. The re-ranked list and a build order are at the end.

## The one fact: a model cannot tell instructions from data

Prompt injection was named in 2022 by analogy to SQL injection, and the analogy is where most
of the field's confusion starts. SQL injection has a fix. A parameterized query sends the code
and the data down two different channels, so no value a user types can ever be parsed as a
command. The bug class did not get rarer because databases learned to spot malicious strings.
It got rarer because the architecture stopped mixing the two.

A language model has one channel. The system prompt, the user's request, the retrieved document,
the tool's output and the web page are all tokens in the same sequence, and the model is trained
to follow instructions wherever they appear. Simon Willison, who named the attack, wrote in 2023
that the "parameterized prompts" idea is "extremely difficult, if not impossible, to implement on
the current architecture of large language models." Two and a half years later, the people whose
job is to have solved it say they have not:

- The UK's **NCSC** (December 2025): "there is no inherent distinction between 'data' and
  'instruction'", so prompt injection "may never be totally mitigated in the way that SQL
  injection attacks can be." Its advice is to treat the model as "an inherently confusable deputy."
- **Anthropic** (November 2025): prompt injection is "far from a solved problem… A 1% attack
  success rate — while a significant improvement — still represents meaningful risk."
- **OpenAI**, hardening its Atlas browser agent in December 2025, called it unlikely ever to be
  fully "solved", comparing it with scams and social engineering of people.

Two consequences follow, and the rest of this post is built on them.

**First, the model is not the security boundary. It is the thing the boundary is drawn around.**
A system prompt that says "never reveal the customer table" is a request to a component that, by
construction, also takes requests from whoever wrote the last document it read. The list is right
that "system prompts are suggestions." The engineering question is what sits outside the model
and holds no matter what the model decides.

**Second, any defense that works by reading text and judging whether it is malicious is a
detector, and detectors lose to an attacker who adapts.** In October 2025, fourteen researchers,
Milad Nasr, Nicholas Carlini and Florian Tramèr among them, took twelve published prompt-injection defenses, most
of which had reported near-zero attack success, and attacked them adaptively, with gradient
search, reinforcement learning and human red-teamers. Most fell to above **90%**. MetaSecAlign
went from **2%** to **96%**. A human red-teaming competition with more than 500 participants broke
**every** scenario. The paper's title states the rule: *The Attacker Moves Second*. A detector
raises the price of an attack, which is worth something. It is not a wall.

This is why "tool poisoning is the SQL injection of the agentic era" teaches the wrong lesson.
Prompt injection, of which tool poisoning is one variant, is shaped like SQL injection *without
the parameterized query*. The bugs in the MCP ecosystem that really are like SQL injection are
the classic ones, and they do have fixes: command injection in `mcp-remote` (CVE-2025-6514,
CVSS 9.6), CSRF to remote code execution in MCP Inspector (CVE-2025-49596, CVSS 9.4), path and
symlink escapes in Anthropic's own Filesystem server, argument injection in its Git server. Fix
those the old way. The new problem needs a different kind of answer.

## What turns confusion into damage: the agent's authority

A chatbot that can be talked into anything can only embarrass you. An agent can be *used*.
The difference is authority, and computer security has had a name for this failure since 1988.
Norm Hardy's "confused deputy" was a compiler that held two kinds of authority: the user's, and
its own right to write a billing file. A user named the billing file as an output, and the
compiler, acting with its own rights on the user's instructions, overwrote it. No one stole a
credential. A program holding legitimate authority was steered by someone who did not hold it.

An agent is that compiler at scale. It acts with the user's authority, through tokens, sessions
and API keys, and it takes instructions from anyone who can write text into its context: the
sender of an email, the author of a GitHub issue, whoever edited a web page. Two short
formulations of when this becomes dangerous have become the field's working threat model:

- **The lethal trifecta** (Willison, June 2025): access to private data, exposure to untrusted
  content, and the ability to communicate externally. Any agent with all three can be made to
  steal the data.
- **The Agents Rule of Two** (Meta, October 2025): within a session, an agent should have *no
  more than two* of [A] processing untrustworthy inputs, [B] access to sensitive systems or
  private data, and [C] the ability to change state or communicate externally. Meta's [C] is
  broader than Willison's third leg. It covers *any* state change, not only exfiltration.

These are not theory. Line up the best-documented agent data leaks of the last two years and
every one of them is the same three ingredients.

Read the table by columns rather than by rows. The first column is the attack surface, and it is
every input the agent reads. The second is the prize, which is whatever its credentials reach.
The third is the getaway. Agentic security engineering is the work of keeping all three from
meeting in one session and narrowing each one where they must. Put precisely, that is four
questions about the path an attacker's text takes:

1. **Where does untrusted text get in?** Every channel into the context window.
2. **Can that text change what the agent decides to do?** The control flow.
3. **What can the agent's actions reach?** Tools, identity, the sandbox.
4. **How can anything get out?** Rendered output, URLs, the network, the model provider.

Two more questions sit off that path. What is the agent built from: its packages, servers,
skills and model files? And how will you know, before and after the fact, whether the other four
held? Here is the whole map, with the list's fifteen projects placed on it.

## Entry: every channel into the context is an instruction channel

Start where the list spends most of its effort. The lesson of this layer is that it is wider
than it looks and that it cannot be sealed, and both halves matter.

**The user's own turns.** Crescendo (Russinovich, Salem and Eldan at Microsoft; USENIX Security
2025) is the reference multi-turn jailbreak. It opens innocently, then escalates by quoting the
model's own previous answers back at it, so that no single turn looks like an attack. Scale AI's
human red-teamers, working over many turns, exceeded **70%** attack success on HarmBench against
defenses that report single-digit rates against automated single-turn attacks. So the list's
project #1, a stateful multi-turn fuzzer, is a real build, and testing only single turns
measures the wrong thing.

But the list's "why" for it, that "single-shot 'ignore instructions' injections are dead", does
not survive the evidence. Crescendo and its relatives are *jailbreaks*: the user is the attacker,
and the harm is mostly content. For agents the larger threat is *indirect* injection, where the
attacker is a third party and one message is often enough. EchoLeak was one email, read with zero
clicks. The GitHub MCP exploit was one issue, which Invariant described as a "relatively
simplistic" injection that beat Claude 4 Opus. A 2026 competition fired **272,000** attacks at
thirteen frontier models and found success rates from **0.5%** to **8.5%** per model. In the UK
AI Security Institute and Gray Swan's 2025 challenge, 1.8 million attacks produced more than
60,000 policy violations, and "nearly all agents exhibit policy violations for most behaviors
within 10–100 queries." Crude override phrasing is rarer than it was. The single shot is not dead.

**Retrieved documents.** PoisonedRAG (USENIX Security 2025) inserted **five** crafted passages per
target question into corpora of up to 8.8 million passages and got the attacker's chosen answer
about **90%** of the time or better. BadRAG reached a 98.2% retrieval rate with ten passages,
0.04% of the corpus. Those numbers are real, but they qualify the list's line that "if an attacker
slips a poisoned document into your knowledge base, they own every answer." Each poisoned passage
owns the answers to the queries that *retrieve it*. If that passage also carries an injection, as
in EchoLeak and ForcedLeak, it owns the *session* that retrieved it, and that is the worse outcome.

That changes what project #5 should do. Checking that each claim matches the hash of a stored
chunk proves provenance, not truth: the poisoned chunk *is* a genuine stored chunk, and the
answer is faithful to it. Carlini and colleagues showed the general form in 2023, poisoning
0.01% of two public web-scale datasets for about sixty dollars. Content hashes stopped content
from changing after it was indexed. They did nothing about poison that was there when the
snapshot was taken. The controls that work at this layer are about who can *write* to the corpus
and who can *read* from it. Ingest from writers you trust, and treat email, forms and shared docs
as attacker-writable by design. Enforce the reader's permissions at retrieval (OWASP lists this as
LLM08). And, at the decision layer, treat whatever was retrieved as data that may not steer actions.

**Memory.** Memory turns a one-time injection into a standing one. Johann Rehberger's SpAIware
(2024) had a web page write instructions into ChatGPT's long-term memory, which then leaked every
later conversation. His Gemini attack (February 2025) planted a memory that fires only when the
user next types "yes", so the tool call appears to come from the user. MINJA (2025) needs no write
access at all: ordinary queries reached **98.2%** injection success into an agent's memory. Memory
poisoning is now ASI06 in OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications. The list's project #11, a
"sleeper-agent scrubber" for vector stores, merges two different things, though. A sleeper agent
(Hubinger et al., 2024) is a backdoor in the *weights*. It persisted through safety training,
and a 2025 study planted a (deliberately harmless) backdoor in models from 600M to 13B parameters
with the same 250 poisoned documents, whatever the model's size. No retrieved chunk contains it. Scanning a store can flag injected text at
rest, which is worth doing, but the stronger controls are structural: untrusted content may not
write memory, every memory carries its source, and memories expire.

**Tool descriptions.** Invariant Labs' tool-poisoning disclosure (April 2025) hid instructions in
an MCP tool's description, which the model reads and the user usually does not. It added the
*rug pull*, in which a server changes a description after the user approved it, and *shadowing*,
in which one server's description rewrites how the agent uses another server's tool. MCPTox,
testing 45 real servers and 353 tools, found attack success of up to **72.8%**, and found that
the more capable models were the *more* susceptible. The fixes are concrete: pin each tool's
description by hash and re-approve on change, and show the user what the model is told.

**Other agents.** In a multi-agent system, one agent's output is another's input. Triedman, Jha and
Shmatikov (COLM 2025) hijacked orchestrators such as Magentic-One into running arbitrary code
in **58–90%** of trials, up to 97% in one configuration, *even when each individual agent resisted
prompt injection*, because the attack rode the control flow between them. That is why project #3,
a bus that "strips malicious instructions" between agents, cannot be a boundary. It is a detector
placed where a detector is weakest. The useful version tags every inter-agent message with where it
came from and lets the receiving side treat it as untrusted data.

**Pixels.** Computer-use agents read screens, so a screen is a prompt. Pop-ups designed to be
clicked by agents got clicked **86%** of the time on OSWorld and VisualWebArena, and telling the
agent to ignore pop-ups did not help. Brave hijacked Perplexity's Comet with faint light-blue text
on a yellow background that a human would not notice in a screenshot. A "pixel auditor"
(project #10) is a vision model judging whether a screen is adversarial, so it has the weakness it
is meant to guard against. Anthropic does ship screenshot classifiers, as one layer, and it pairs
them with per-site permissions, blocked site categories and confirmation before high-risk
actions. With those, its browser agent's attack success fell from **23.6%** to **11.2%** in
August 2025.

The pattern across all six channels is the same. Every control at this layer *lowers a rate*.
Anthropic's adaptive attacker, given a hundred attempts per environment, still had a success
rate of **1.4%** against Claude Opus 4.5 with the improved safeguards, down from 8.0% for the model
alone. That is real progress, and it is not zero. Since the entry layer cannot be closed, the
defense that matters has to work *after* the injection has already succeeded.

## Decision: keep untrusted text away from control flow

This is the layer the list leaves out, and it is the one that can give guarantees. The
principle comes from *Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections*
(Beurer-Kellner and thirteen co-authors, 2025):

> once an LLM agent has ingested untrusted input, it must be constrained so that it is
> impossible for that input to trigger any consequential actions.

The point is to stop asking whether the model will notice the injection. Arrange things so that
it does not matter whether it notices. The paper gives six patterns, and they all do one thing:
they decide the agent's *actions* before, or apart from, the moment it reads untrusted data.

- **Action-selector.** The model maps a request onto a fixed menu of actions and never sees what
  they return. It is immune to injection, and also mostly unable to do anything clever.
- **Plan-then-execute.** The plan is fixed from the trusted request before any untrusted data is
  read. Injected text can no longer add or reorder steps, but it can still alter their
  *arguments*: what goes into the body of the email that the plan says to send.
- **Dual LLM.** A privileged model plans and holds the tools but never reads untrusted text. A
  quarantined model reads it but holds no tools. It returns results as opaque variables that
  ordinary code, not the planner, puts into tool calls.
- **Code-then-execute, map-reduce, context-minimization.** These are the same idea applied to
  programs, to batches of documents, and to the user's own prompt.

**CaMeL** (Google DeepMind and ETH Zurich, 2025) is the strongest form. The privileged model
writes a small program from the user's request alone. The quarantined model parses untrusted
data. A custom interpreter tags every value with where it came from and checks a policy at every
tool call: *may data from this email become the recipient of `send_email`?* On AgentDojo it
completed **77%** of tasks with provable security, against **84%** with no defense at all.
**FIDES** (Microsoft, 2025) does the same with confidentiality and integrity labels on a planner.

Two cautions keep this honest. What CaMeL proves is limited to control flow and data flow under
the policies you wrote, so a bad policy is still a bad policy. And the guarantee costs
generality: an independent 2026 re-measurement put CaMeL's utility at about 30% on AgentDojo and
**zero** on a newer benchmark of unfamiliar environments. The design-patterns paper states the
trade plainly: "securing general-purpose agents remains out of reach with current capabilities,"
but "application-specific agents can be secured through principled system design."

Take the practice task from stage 1 of the curriculum: an agent that reads email and writes to a
CRM. Reading email is untrusted input [A]. The CRM holds customer data [B]. Writing to it is a
state change [C]. Built the obvious way, it has all three, so it fails the Rule of Two before a
line of code is written. Here is the same agent built so that a successful injection has nowhere
to go.

## Action: make the deputy small

When the decision layer cannot be fully isolated, and in a general-purpose agent it usually
cannot, the next question is what the agent's hands can reach. Projects #2 and #7 belong here,
and both need one correction.

**Validating a call's shape is not authorizing it.** Project #2 is an MCP proxy that "validates
parameters via Pydantic and blocks confused deputy privilege escalations." Type validation does
catch something real: Anthropic's Git MCP server had an argument-injection bug, CVE-2025-68144,
that a strict schema would have stopped. But a hijacked agent does not send malformed calls. It
sends perfect ones. `create_pull_request(repo="public-repo", body="<the private code>")` validates
cleanly. In the GitHub MCP exploit, the token was legitimately scoped to both repositories, and
Invariant called it "not a flaw in the GitHub MCP server code itself" but "a fundamental
architectural issue." In the Supabase case, the agent ran with a role that bypasses row-level
security, and every query it made was permitted. The MCP specification's own security guidance
lists the mistake by name: "treating claimed scopes in token as sufficient without server-side
authorization logic."

So the proxy is worth building, but its job is *authorization against the task*, and the
question it has to answer is whether this call fits what this session was opened to do:

- **Pin the session.** Invariant's own mitigation for the GitHub exploit was one repository per
  session. The general form is the Rule of Two enforced in the proxy: a session that has read
  untrusted content loses the tools that write externally.
- **Check where arguments came from.** A recipient, URL or file path that arrived in untrusted
  content gets refused or escalated. This is CaMeL's provenance check, done without CaMeL.
- **Pin tool definitions.** Hash every tool description at approval, and reject a server whose
  descriptions change. That closes the rug pull.
- **Deny by default.** Expose the three tools the task needs, not the forty the server offers.

**Give the agent its own identity, then narrow it.** Project #7 is right that agents "should
never hold the master keys", and the standards to build it now exist. The MCP authorization spec
(revised through 2025 and again in July 2026) builds on OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and requires
audience-bound tokens (RFC 8707). It is blunt about relaying credentials: "The MCP server MUST NOT
pass through the token it received from the MCP client." OAuth token exchange (RFC 8693) lets the
agent act *on behalf of* a user while keeping a separate identity in the token's `act` claim, so
the logs say "agent X for user Y" rather than "user Y". DPoP (RFC 9449) binds a token to a key,
so a stolen token cannot be replayed, and CIBA lets the agent ask the human to approve an action
on their own phone.

All of that limits the *blast radius*. None of it stops misuse *within* scope. In both the GitHub
and Supabase incidents, a perfectly scoped, audience-bound, unstolen token did exactly what the
injected agent asked. Delegated identity is necessary. The task-level policy in the proxy is what
makes it sufficient.

**Human approval is a scarce resource.** "Ask the user" is the default answer for consequential
actions, and the data says it wears out. Anthropic found that Claude Code users accept **93%** of
permission prompts. Its answer has been *fewer and better* prompts, not more warnings: an
OS-level sandbox cut prompts by **84%** internally, and the lesson it drew was that "effective sandboxing
requires both filesystem and network isolation." An approval should be rare, specific and
out-of-band. Ask "Send 4 records to an external address?", not "Allow tool call?"

**The sandbox has to hold against your own agent.** In August 2025, the malicious Nx package
"s1ngularity" did not need to break any AI tool. It found Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Amazon Q
already installed, ran them with their permission-skipping flags, and asked them to hunt for
secrets. More than a thousand valid GitHub tokens leaked. An agent's permissions are a capability
that anything on the machine can borrow. The sandbox, not the agent's good judgment, decides what
that borrowing reaches.

## The exits: close the ways data leaves

Look again at the last column of Figure 1. Most of those leaks did not need the agent to call a
send tool. They needed something to *fetch a URL*, usually an image that the chat client loaded
by itself, with the stolen data in the query string. That channel has been reported and fixed,
product by product, since Bing Chat in 2023, and it keeps coming back, because every fix is an
allow-list and an allow-list is only as strong as the weakest thing on it. EchoLeak shows the
whole problem in four steps.

The durable fixes do not try to guess which URLs are bad. They remove the ability to construct
new ones. Since early 2026, OpenAI's agents auto-fetch a URL only if an independent web index has
already seen that *exact* URL, not merely its domain, because the attacker's version, with the
secret in it, has never been crawled. Its Deep Research agent may not construct URLs at all. Even
this leaves a trickle: researchers showed that a set of pre-indexed URLs, one per character, can
still spell out a secret slowly. The general rule is to give the output renderer no
auto-loading images from anywhere you do not control, and to send the agent's network traffic
through an egress proxy that knows which destinations the task needs.

**Grammar constraints are physics for form, not for meaning.** Project #6 cages output with a
context-free grammar so that the model "physically" cannot emit a link or a code block. The
mechanism is real: constrained decoding masks every token the grammar forbids, so a JSON schema or
Lark grammar is enforced at sampling time, which is stronger than any instruction. But the guarantee
is about *syntax*. A grammar that allows a free-text field allows `https://attacker.example/?q=`
followed by the secret inside it, and a perfectly grammatical `send_email(to=...)` is still a
successful attack. Constraints become real security only where they shrink the *information* the
output can carry. An enum of five values carries at most 2.3 bits. A 280-character free string
carries a password. That is why, in Figure 3, only the typed fields reach the policy, and the one
free-text field is stored where no exit can reach it.

The list also misses that the schema itself is an attack surface. Zhang and colleagues (accepted at
CCS 2026) hid harmful requests inside a structured-output schema while the prompt stayed
benign, and reached **94–99%** attack success on GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-R1 and
gpt-oss-120b, and **75.8%** against current guardrails. If users or third parties can influence the
schema, the grammar is input, and it needs the same scrutiny as any other input.

**The PII gateway is an exit control, and the deterministic version leaks.** Project #4 swaps SSNs
and card numbers for "deterministic UUIDs" before the prompt leaves for a frontier API. The goal,
that raw identifiers never leave your boundary, is right. Three details decide whether it is met:

- **Unkeyed determinism can be reversed.** There are fewer than a billion possible SSNs. If the
  token is an unkeyed hash, and a name-based UUID (version 5) is exactly that, SHA-1 of a namespace
  and the value, anyone holding a token can hash every possible SSN and match it in seconds on one
  GPU. Use a keyed HMAC, or random tokens kept in a vault. PCI DSS 4.0 has required *keyed* hashes
  for stored card numbers since March 2025.
- **It is still personal data, for you.** GDPR Recital 26 and the EDPB's January 2025 guidelines
  say pseudonymised data that can be linked back remains personal data. The EU Court of Justice's
  SRB ruling (September 2025) added that it may *not* be personal data for a recipient with no
  means to re-identify it, which helps with the provider. It does not change your own obligations.
  "Zero trust" is an architecture (NIST SP 800-207), not a compliance status.
- **You can only swap what you detect.** Microsoft's Presidio, the usual open-source detector,
  says in its own documentation that there is "no guarantee" it will find all sensitive data. An
  SSN typed with odd spacing, or a name in a free-text note, passes straight through.

The control to pair it with is contractual: zero-data-retention terms with the model provider,
which Anthropic and OpenAI both offer on eligible endpoints. Swapping reduces what you send.
Retention terms limit what happens to what still gets sent.

## Off the path: what the agent is built from, and the model itself

**Supply chain** is the list's project #13, and it holds up as written. Models invent package
names, and they invent them repeatably, which turns a hallucination into a target. Spracklen and
colleagues (USENIX Security 2025) generated 576,000 code samples from 16 models and found
**205,474** distinct package names that did not exist. When they re-ran prompts ten times, **43%**
of the invented names came back every time. An attacker who registers those names is waiting where
the next model will send its users. When Bar Lanyado registered one name that models kept
recommending, `huggingface-cli`, as an empty package, it collected more than 15,000 downloads in
three months, some of them from developers following a README in an Alibaba repository.

Agent extensions are the same problem one level up. `postmark-mcp`, the first malicious MCP server
found in the wild (September 2025), published fifteen clean versions, then added a single line that
blind-copied every email the agent sent to an outside address. Koi Security audited 2,857 skills on
ClawHub, the marketplace for the OpenClaw agent, in February 2026 and found **341** malicious ones,
most of them in a single campaign that installed password stealers through fake "prerequisite"
commands. Signing helps with *who*: OpenSSF's model-signing 1.0 (2025) and the MCP Registry's
verified namespaces say who published an artifact. They say nothing about whether it is benign. So
pin versions, review diffs on update, and run each server with only the credentials it needs.

**Project #9 defends the model, and it names the wrong threat.** Recovering weights through an API
is mostly impossible. The famous exception, Carlini et al.'s ICML 2024 best paper, recovered one
layer, the final embedding projection, of two OpenAI models for under twenty dollars. It was fixed
by changing the API surface, restricting log-probabilities and logit bias, not by rate limits. The
real threat to a model's value is *distillation*: training a competitor on its outputs. In
February 2026, Anthropic reported campaigns that ran more than **16 million** exchanges through
about **24,000** fraudulent accounts, one proxy network running over 20,000 accounts at once. A
per-account limit on embedding similarity misses traffic that is diverse by design and spread
across thousands of accounts. What Anthropic reported using instead was classifiers and behavioral
fingerprinting across accounts, detection of attempts to elicit chain-of-thought, stricter
verification for account types abused at scale, and sharing indicators with other labs. Build
project #9 as account-graph analytics, not a similarity gate.

**Project #14 is research, not an engineering control, and its target is overstated.** No published
work locates "deceptive alignment" in specific attention heads. Steering vectors for sycophancy
exist (Rimsky et al., 2024), and probes are genuinely useful. Apollo's linear deception probes
reached AUROC 0.96–0.999 on Llama-3.3-70B, but the authors' own conclusion is that "current
performance is insufficient as a robust defence against deception." Probes can be evaded: one
obfuscation attack cut a harmfulness probe's recall from 100% to 0% while keeping the jailbreak
working. And ablating one component often just moves the behavior elsewhere in the network. The
honest place for this work in a security program is as a *monitor*. Anthropic's 2026
Constitutional Classifiers use a cheap activation probe as the first stage of a cascade. That
requires access to the weights, so for most teams calling a closed API it is not available at all.

## Evidence: knowing before, proving after

**A red-team gate in CI is a regression test, so build it like one.** Project #8 runs 1,000
PyRIT payloads on every pull request and blocks the merge if the jailbreak rate exceeds 1%.
Automated adversarial testing in CI is right. The number is where it goes wrong. With 1,000
trials, a threshold at 1% sits inside the noise.

Three more things weaken the number. Sampling is random, so one payload sampled once is a single
coin toss: a payload that works 5% of the time per try succeeds at least once in ten tries
**40%** of the time, and an attacker gets as many tries as they like. Payloads come in families of
near-duplicates, so 1,000 payloads are fewer than 1,000 independent trials. And the LLM judge that
scores them makes errors of its own. Microsoft's red team, reporting on more than 100 products,
notes that LLM judges are least reliable in specialist domains such as cybersecurity.

The deeper problem is what the gate measures. A fixed suite measures robustness *to those
payloads*. That is exactly the setting in which the twelve defenses in *The Attacker Moves Second*
reported near-zero success before adaptive attacks took most of them above 90%. So build the gate
as what it is, a regression test:

- **Compare against the last release**, not a fixed threshold, and give each payload several tries.
- **Size N for the decision.** Set the cut-off so a true 0.5% rate is rarely blocked, and 1,000
  trials catch a true 1% rate only 54% of the time. It takes about 5,000 to catch it 99% of the time.
- **Calibrate the judge** on a set labelled by people, and report the calibration with the result.
- **Run AgentDojo-style task suites,** which measure injected *actions* and not only harmful text.
- **Schedule adaptive red-teaming** by people and by optimizing attackers, outside CI. Microsoft's
  lessons are explicit that automation "should not be used with the intention of taking the human
  out of the loop."

Project #1, the Crescendo fuzzer, is the adaptive half of this. It belongs in the scheduled
campaign, not in the merge gate.

**A hash-chained log proves integrity, not why.** Project #12 is an append-only ledger of every
prompt, retrieved chunk, tool call and state change. It is worth building, and it is the
project most teams will be asked for first. The list's promise that it gives "cryptographic proof
of exactly why it happened" overreaches in three ways:

- A hash chain proves that entries were not changed *after* they were written. It cannot show
  that every event was written, or that what was written is true: a compromised host logs what
  it likes.
- Even integrity needs an outside anchor. Certificate Transparency's own specification (RFC 9162)
  warns that a log can show different views of itself to different readers, unless its head is
  published or witnessed somewhere the operator does not control.
- A model's logged reasoning is not a faithful record of its cause.

What the ledger can give you is a *replayable record of inputs*. It shows which chunk IDs were
retrieved, which tool definitions (by hash) were loaded, which policy allowed each call, and what
each call returned. With that you can rebuild the context and rerun the decision, which is the
closest thing to "why" there is. Record the policy decisions, not only the model's actions. Use
OpenTelemetry's GenAI agent spans as the schema, though they are still marked "Development".

Two constraints shape it. The EU AI Act requires automatic event logging for high-risk systems
(Article 12), kept for at least six months by deployers (Article 26). The 2026 Digital Omnibus
moved those high-risk obligations to **2 December 2027** for stand-alone systems and **2 August
2028** for systems built into regulated products. A ledger that stores full prompts also stores
the personal data in them, and GDPR's storage limits still apply, so redact or pseudonymise at
write time and keep retention tiered.

**A teardown is worth publishing when it crosses a trust boundary.** Project #15, publishing
disclosures, is how this field's knowledge actually moved, and almost every incident in this post
began as one. The vendors have converged on where the line is. Google's AI bug bounty and
Microsoft's both exclude jailbreaks that only affect the attacker's own session. Injection that
reaches *another* user's data, takes an unauthorized action or executes code is a vulnerability,
and it gets a CVE: EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711), or CVE-2025-53773, in which an injected prompt made
GitHub Copilot write `"chat.tools.autoApprove": true` into the workspace settings and then run
commands. Aim teardowns at that line.

## The list, re-ranked

Here are all fifteen projects again, each placed on the map, with a verdict and the corrected
reason. **Build** means as stated. **Reframe** means the attack surface is real but the project
defends the wrong thing or claims the wrong guarantee. **Demote** means a detector or research
tool listed as if it were a control.

| # | Project | Layer | Verdict | The corrected why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Crescendo fuzzer | Evidence | Build | Multi-turn grooming is real. Run it as a scheduled adaptive campaign. Single-shot *indirect* injection is still the larger threat to agents. |
| 2 | MCP proxy | Action | Reframe | Authorize each call against the session's task and the provenance of its arguments, and pin tool definitions by hash. Schema validation is the smaller half. |
| 3 | Inter-agent bus | Entry | Demote | Stripping instructions is detection. Tag each message with its source and treat it as untrusted data. |
| 4 | PII gateway | Exit | Reframe | Keyed or vaulted tokens, never unkeyed determinism. It is still personal data for you. Pair it with zero-retention terms. |
| 5 | RAG poison detector | Entry | Reframe | Hashes prove provenance, not truth. Control who can write to the corpus and enforce the reader's permissions. |
| 6 | Grammar cage | Exit | Reframe | Grammars fix form, not meaning. They are a real control only where they shrink information, and the schema is itself an input. |
| 7 | Agent OAuth broker | Action | Build | Token exchange, audience binding, no passthrough. It limits blast radius, not misuse within scope. |
| 8 | CI red-team gate | Evidence | Reframe | A regression test. Compare against the last release, size N for the decision, and calibrate the judge. |
| 9 | Semantic rate limiter | Supply | Reframe | The threat is distillation across thousands of accounts, not weight theft. Build account-graph analytics. |
| 10 | Pixel auditor | Entry | Demote | One classifier layer. Acting on DOM targets, site permissions and confirmations do the work. |
| 11 | Sleeper-agent scrubber | Entry | Reframe | Sleeper agents live in weights. For memory stores, gate writes, record sources, and expire entries. |
| 12 | Trajectory ledger | Evidence | Build | A replayable record of inputs and policy decisions, anchored externally. Not proof of "why". |
| 13 | SBOM scanner | Supply | Build | Hallucinated names recur, and extensions turn malicious after trust. Pin versions and review diffs. |
| 14 | Activation patching | Supply | Demote | Research. Probes are monitors with known evasions, need the weights, and no head-level deception circuit is known. |
| 15 | Public teardowns | Evidence | Build | Aim at trust-boundary crossings, the class vendors treat as vulnerabilities. |

Two things are missing from the fifteen, and they are the two that do the most work. The first
is **decision-layer isolation**: plan-then-execute, the dual LLM, CaMeL-style provenance
tracking. It is the only layer where a successful injection can be made harmless rather than
less likely. The second is **the sandbox and the egress proxy**: an execution boundary and a
network boundary that hold even when the agent has been turned against you.

## A build order

The order follows from the map. Start where guarantees are possible, and add rate-lowering
controls last, because they matter least on their own.

1. **Threat-model every session with the Rule of Two.** For each agent, list which of untrusted
   input, sensitive access and outbound action a session holds. Any session with all three gets
   redesigned, as in Figure 3, before anything else is built.
2. **Isolate the decision.** Fix the plan from trusted input, quarantine untrusted text, type every
   field that crosses back.
3. **Shrink the hands.** An authorizing proxy (#2), delegated narrow tokens (#7), an OS sandbox
   with filesystem and network isolation.
4. **Close the exits.** No auto-loading external content in the renderer, an egress allow-list,
   PII tokenized with keys (#4), and grammars where they cut information (#6).
5. **Record and test.** The ledger (#12), the regression gate (#8), and a scheduled adaptive
   campaign (#1).
6. **Watch the supply chain** continuously (#13), and defend the model as an asset if you serve one (#9).
7. **Add detectors** (#3, #5, #10, #11) as telemetry that feeds the ledger and raises the
   attacker's cost, never as the thing that holds.

The field is real, and the reason is less flattering than the list's promise that you "will never
be unemployed again." The central problem has no known fix, so the work does not end. Microsoft's
red team, after more than a hundred products, put it as its eighth lesson: "The work of securing
AI systems will never be complete." The engineering that lasts does not count on winning that
argument with the model. It decides what the model can do while it is still losing it.
